title: Mrs. Henderson Presents
full_review:
Some may remember the old Rita Hayworth musical, "Tonight & Every Night," which concerned London's Windmill Theatre, the only one to stay open throughout the dangerous period of the blitz during World War II. Of course, what you don't see in that Turner Classic Movies staple are topless showgirls, but that indeed was the featured attraction of the theater.

"Mrs. Henderson Presents" (Pathe/BBC) is the patriotic true-life story -- well, "inspired by" true events -- of how wealthy widow Laura Henderson (Judi Dench), at odds with life after the death of her husband in 1937, refurbishes a dilapidated movie theater to put on musical revues.

She knows nothing of managing theaters or mounting shows, so she hires an artistic director, Vivian Van Damm (Bob Hoskins, who also produced the film).

"Revudeville," as it's called, is so successful that copycat theaters steal the Windmill's winning vaudeville formula of four shows a day, causing box office receipts to dwindle. This prompts the indefatigable Mrs. Henderson to suggest introducing discreet nudity into the shows, modeled on the Moulin Rouge in Paris.

Using all her charm on the official censor, the Lord Chamberlain (Christopher Guest), she convinces him of the merits of the conceit, which lead him to grant his permission, provided the girls remain absolutely stationary in artistic tableaux.

The new format is a triumph, and the crowds return. Once war breaks out, and the Germans begin their onslaught, the Windmill becomes a refuge from the death and destruction around them -- and, as the auditorium is underground, relatively safe. When the bombing intensifies, Mrs. Henderson even has the girls sleep there overnight.

Mrs. Henderson is quite smitten with "Mr. Van Damm," as she calls him, a man she guesses is a Dutch Jew, a fact that will become poignantly clear when the Germans invade Holland later on, but when she learns he has a wife she becomes childishly resentful. But the platonic relationship never goes beyond the mutual respect of two people who seem polar opposites.

At one point, the romantically minded Mrs. Henderson encourages one of the girls, Maureen (Kelly Reilly), to go out with a soldier. Against her better judgment, Maureen does, with unhappy consequences.

Eventually, the theater runs afoul of the Lord Chamberlain -- now viewing the enterprise as a frivolous distraction -- leading to a battle of wills. Mrs. Henderson's rabble-rousing speech at the end, in which she passionately argues for the show to carry on, contains some questionable moral logic. Still, it can't be denied that the Windmill did provide a morale-boosting service, and was so respectable (as were the girls themselves) that it attracted families with children -- and even, on occasion, royalty.

Despite the seeming raciness of the theme, and several artfully posed tableaux, the proceedings are basically as decorous as anything on "Masterpiece Theatre." There is a more risque sight gag where the girls must first remove their clothing, and will only do so if the few men in the theater do so as well. Dame Judi walks in to see a blink-and-you-miss-it glimpse of everyone, including Hoskins, in the altogether.

Stephen Frears' well-made film, with a script by playwright Martin Sherman, tugs at the heartstrings, and presents a convincing recreation -- musical numbers and all -- of a small but significant chapter in London's brave resistance to Hitler's relentless bombardment.

There are predictably fine performances by the leads. This is one of Dench's biggest parts, and she has a field day with it, and Hoskins, using a posher accent than usual, is equally accomplished.

Viewed in the proper historical context, "Mrs. Henderson Presents" makes diverting adult viewing.

The film has partial female nudity throughout, and a fleeting scene of full-frontal male and female nudity, a premarital affair with tragic results, some innuendo, a smattering of profanity and rough language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
